In Basic Science, what exactly is a cell?

A cell is the smallest unit of a living thing that can carry out life processes. Every living organism, whether a tiny ant, a mango tree, or a human being, is made up of cells. Because it is the basic building block from which all living things are made, we call the cell the 'basic unit of life'. Some organisms, like bacteria, are made of just one cell and are called unicellular. Others, like humans, are made of billions of cells and are called multicellular. You cannot see a single cell with your naked eye; you need a microscope. Just as a house is built from many blocks, your body is built from many cells working together.

What are the three main parts of a cell?

A typical cell has three main parts.

First, the CELL MEMBRANE is the thin outer covering that holds the cell together and controls what enters and leaves it, like a gatekeeper.
Second, the CYTOPLASM is the jelly-like fluid inside the cell where most life activities happen and where tiny structures float.
Third, the NUCLEUS is the dark, rounded structure that acts as the control centre or 'brain' of the cell, directing all its activities and carrying the hereditary material. Think of the cell as a compound: the membrane is the fence, the cytoplasm is the open space where work happens, and the nucleus is the head of the household giving instructions. These three parts are found in nearly every cell.

How does a plant cell differ from an animal cell?

Plant cells and animal cells share the membrane, cytoplasm and nucleus, but a plant cell has three extra features.

First, a CELL WALL, a tough layer outside the membrane that gives the plant cell a fixed, boxy shape and support; animal cells have no cell wall, so they are more rounded and flexible.
Second, CHLOROPLASTS, the green structures containing chlorophyll that trap sunlight to make food; animal cells have none, which is why animals cannot make their own food.
Third, a large permanent VACUOLE filled with cell sap that stores water and keeps the plant firm; animal cells have only small, temporary vacuoles.

So remember: cell wall, chloroplasts and a big vacuole belong to plant cells. That is why a leaf is green and firm, but your skin is soft.

What job does the nucleus do inside the cell?

The nucleus is the control centre of the cell, and it has two main jobs.

First, it directs and controls all the activities of the cell, such as growth, feeding and repair, rather like a head teacher directing a whole school.
Second, it carries the hereditary material called chromosomes, which hold the instructions passed from parents to offspring; this is why children resemble their parents. The nucleus is usually the most visible structure inside a cell when you look through a microscope, appearing as a dark rounded body in the cytoplasm. Without a nucleus, a cell cannot control itself or reproduce properly.

So although it is just one part, the nucleus is the most important manager of the cell's life.

What does the cell membrane do?

The cell membrane is the thin covering around the cell, and it has two important functions.

First, it holds the cell together and gives it a boundary, keeping the cytoplasm and other parts safely inside.
Second, and most importantly, it controls what moves into and out of the cell; it allows useful things like food and oxygen to enter and lets waste products leave, while keeping out harmful substances. Because it allows some things through but not others, we say it is selectively permeable, like a careful gateman who checks everyone before letting them into a compound. This control keeps the inside of the cell in the right condition for life. Every cell, plant or animal, has this vital membrane.

What is a tissue and how is it related to cells?

A tissue is a group of similar cells working together to do a particular job. Cells rarely work alone; they join with others of the same kind to form a tissue. For example, many muscle cells together form muscle tissue, which helps the body move, and many nerve cells form nerve tissue, which carries messages. This shows a level of organisation in living things: cells make up tissues, tissues make up organs like the heart or a leaf, organs make up systems like the digestive system, and systems make up the whole organism. Think of it like a school: one pupil is a cell, a class is a tissue, a department is an organ, and the whole school is the organism. Each level is built from the one below it.

Why do we need a microscope to see cells?

We need a microscope because cells are extremely small, far too tiny to be seen with the naked eye. A single cell may be only a few thousandths of a millimetre across. A microscope is an instrument that uses lenses to magnify objects, making them appear many times larger so we can study their parts. When you place a thin slice of onion skin under a microscope, the tiny box-like plant cells suddenly become visible, complete with their walls and nuclei. Before the microscope was invented, people had no idea that living things were made of cells. So the microscope opened up a hidden world. In your science practical, learning to handle the microscope carefully lets you see this world of cells for yourself.

Why is the cell called the basic unit of life?

The cell is called the basic unit of life for two clear reasons.

First, it is the smallest part of a living thing that is still alive and can carry out all the processes of life, such as feeding, breathing, growing and reproducing. Anything smaller than a cell, like a single part of it, cannot live on its own.
Second, every living organism is built from cells; there is no living thing that is not made of at least one cell. Just as bricks are the basic units from which a wall is built, cells are the basic units from which all living bodies are built.

So whether we look at a blade of grass or a human being, we always find cells as the foundation. That is why biology begins with the cell.
